content.headline: Model it once. Every engine reads it.
content.subheadline: Hatamoto is a schema-first CMS. You define entities, and the same model drives your pages, JSON-LD, sitemaps and llms.txt. SEO, AI answer visibility, analytics and caching ship in core. You don't have to bolt on plugins to get them.

content.heading: The plugin stack you'd normally assemble, already in the box.
content.subheading: Each of these comes with Hatamoto out of the box and reads from the same entity model. Your schema markup can't drift from your sitemap, and your sitemap can't drift from the page.

features.title: Schema-first entities
features.description: Content types are JSON Schemas with schema.org annotations, plus a URL pattern. You edit them in the admin. Pages, posts, services and locations are all entities.

features.title: A Tiptap editor that knows your site
features.description: Rich text with tables, images, bubble and floating menus, HTML blocks, and entity links that stay valid when a slug changes.
features.tags: tiptap · html blocks · entity links · scheduling

features.title: Built for answer engines
features.description: Typed JSON-LD for every entity, FAQ and Claim markup, a knowledge graph endpoint, and llms.txt with per-page opt-out.

features.title: SEO isn't an add-on
features.description: Every entity gets meta and canonical fields. Redirects are managed in the admin with 301 to 308, misses go to a 404 log, and rule-based internal links are built in.

features.title: Media library
features.description: Upload once. Hatamoto validates the file, creates resized variants and encodes WebP, and you can pick the image straight from the editor.

features.title: First-party analytics
features.description: Pageviews and AI-assistant referrals are rolled up per day in your own Postgres, with no cookies and no visitor records. Known bots are filtered out.

features.title: Agent analytics
features.description: See which AI crawlers and assistants fetch your pages, why they fetch them, and whether the traffic is really from them.

features.title: Caching built in
features.description: An in-process cache holds rendered pages and sitemaps and is cleared when content changes. You don't need an extra cache plugin.

features.title: Sitemaps that know your content
features.description: A sitemap index with a sub-sitemap for each content group, an XSL view for humans, and a sitemap.urls hook for plugins.

content.headline: Search engines and LLMs read structure. Write it once, at the source.
content.body:
Most CMSs store a page as a block of HTML and leave plugins to guess what it means afterwards. One plugin adds the schema markup, another builds the sitemap, and a third writes llms.txt. They all read the same page and they all reach slightly different conclusions.

Hatamoto works the other way round. You describe the thing first, for example a service, a location or a person, and say which schema.org type it is. The public page, the structured data, the sitemap entry and the AI summary are all generated from that one record, so they can't contradict each other.

Typed fields, not page soup

Fields are validated against the schema when you save. Rich text is sanitised on the way in, so it stays clean even when a plugin edits it through the entity.before_save filter.

URLs are part of the model

Each schema owns its URL pattern. Paths, archives and canonical URLs are worked out from the model, and redirects pick up the slack when content moves.
content.asideText: Entities first. Every page is a typed record before it is HTML.

content.heading: Rank in search. Get cited in answers.
content.lede: Classic SEO and AI answer visibility need the same thing: clean, structured, verifiable content. Hatamoto handles both from the core.

rows.description: Generated from the schema for every entity, with FAQPage, Question, Answer and Claim markup. Plugins can enrich it through the jsonld.enrich filter.
Served from the same model, with a summary for each entity and a per-page switch for content you'd rather leave out.
A public endpoint that shows how your entities relate to each other.
Rule-based link suggestions that you can preview and then insert into the editor with one click.
Admin-managed 301, 302, 307 and 308 rules, checked before page routing, with a 404 log so nothing slips through.

content.heading: Know when an AI reads your page, and why.

content.heading: One model instead of a plugin stack.
content.subheading: Every plugin you add brings its own settings screen, its own update schedule and its own idea of what the page means. Hatamoto keeps all of that in one place.

First-party analytics in your own Postgres
AI agent visits tracked on the server

content.heading: Extend it with one import.
content.lede: Plugins import a single package, hatamoto/core/pkg/sdk. It has its own go.mod and depends only on chi, pgx and the standard library. Typed hooks, a manifest, and you're wired in.
content.footnote: Plugins can also ship goose migrations, a settings form generated from a JSON Schema, admin and public bundles, and role-gated routes. A plugin that fails to wire is reported in the admin. The server still boots.

faqs.question: What does schema-first mean in Hatamoto?
faqs.answer: Every content type is a JSON Schema annotated with a schema.org type. Pages, JSON-LD, sitemap entries and llms.txt summaries are all generated from the same typed record, so they stay in sync.

faqs.question: Do I need plugins for SEO, sitemaps or caching?
faqs.answer: No. Meta and canonical fields, redirects, a 404 log, internal linking, sitemaps with hreflang, llms.txt, caching and first-party analytics all ship in core.

faqs.question: What is agent analytics?
faqs.answer: Server-side tracking of AI crawlers and assistants. Hatamoto already logs known AI bots today. The next release adds purpose classification, IP verification and per-entity reporting.

faqs.question: How do plugins work?
faqs.answer: A plugin imports one Go package, hatamoto/core/pkg/sdk, registers itself in init() and subscribes to typed hooks. It can ship its own migrations, settings schema and admin or public bundles.

faqs.question: What does Hatamoto run on?
faqs.answer: A Go API, a Next.js 14 front end, Postgres. docker compose up boots the whole stack locally.

content.headline: Stand close. Serve well.
content.subheadline: An open-source CMS for teams who want to be found by search engines and cited by AI, without managing a pile of plugins.
